props.title: Strange Brew

sections.content: Strange Brew brilliantly translates Shakespeare's Hamlet into beer-soaked Canadian comedy, with Bob and Doug McKenzie (Rick Moranis and Dave Thomas) stumbling into corporate conspiracy at Elsinore Brewery. The film evolved from SCTV's popular Great White North segments, where the McKenzie brothers satirized Canadian stereotypes. Like Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure (1989) and Wayne's World (1992), it proved sketch characters could sustain feature-length stories while preserving their loveable idiocy.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it combines lowbrow humor with clever Shakespeare references. Like Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (1990), it retells a classic through the eyes of minor characters. Bob and Doug are essentially Rosencrantz and Guildenstern by way of Cheech and Chong's Up in Smoke (1978) - bumbling witnesses to tragedy who are too buzzed to realize the gravity of events around them.

Strange Brew kicked off a golden age of Canadian comedy crossover success. Its DNA can be seen in later hits like Kids in the Hall: Brain Candy (1996) and Fubar (2002) - films that embrace regional identity while poking loving fun at cultural stereotypes. The McKenzie brothers' "hoser" routine influenced everything from Canadian Bacon (1995) to Trailer Park Boys: The Movie (2006). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: While often dismissed as mere beer-addled slapstick, Strange Brew pioneered the meta-comedy approach later seen in films like Hot Fuzz (2007) and Shaun of the Dead (2004). The McKenzie brothers frequently break the fourth wall, comment on film conventions, and even rewind scenes - techniques that would become hallmarks of postmodern comedy. Their "beauty, eh" catchphrases entered pop culture alongside Ghostbusters (1984) and Caddyshack (1980) quotables.
